plan.title: feat(release): report local-vs-released CLI drift after a release instead of staying silent

narratives.Description: feat(release): report local-vs-released CLI drift after a release instead of staying silent
narratives.Overview:
## Summary

`task release` ships the packages and stops. It never tells the operator that the machine which just cut the release is running a different version — which is reliably the stalest install in the fleet.

Tonight the release machine was on **0.95.0 from 2026-08-04** while cutting **0.107.0**. Twelve versions behind, three weeks stale, and every agent hook on that box was executing August code all day.

Recut after a design critique (successor lean 5420874337). **The remedy changed.** The original proposal was a final step that upgrades the global CLI by default, opt-out. That is refuted. This issue is now: *report the drift where the pipeline is currently silent.*

## Why report and not upgrade

Four reasons, each measured rather than argued.

**Nothing in the pipeline writes global state, and nothing can undo it.** `runPipeline` is 13 steps ending at GitHub draft verify. `task release:rollback` unwinds the GitHub release, tag, and assets — it has no npm retraction and no prefix undo. The closed-verb grant at the Step 10-11 boundary authorizes a tag push and an npm publish, not a write under the operator's own npm prefix. Those are different consents.

**The blast radius is every live agent on the machine, mid-flight.** Measured on the reporting host: `npm config get prefix` is `AppData\Roaming\npm`, `deft-hook` resolves inside it, and `.cursor/hooks.json` invokes the bare command at six call sites. A default upgrade swaps the binary underneath every running session, worktree, and hook with no ritual re-arm. #3233 further records that `npm i -g` can land under one prefix while a higher-precedence PATH entry keeps serving the old CLI, so a bare `deft --version` check would report success on a shadowed install.

**It contradicts a consent rule the framework already enforces.** The sync skill forbids a global upgrade without staleness evidence *and* operator consent, and the staleness tickler mutates only after an interactive yes. A silent opt-out step 14 is exactly the mutation the rest of the framework declines to perform unprompted.

**It would fire during rehearsal.** `task release:e2e` calls the same `runPipeline` at `REHEARSAL_VERSION = "0.0.1"` with only `--skip-ci --skip-build --allow-vbrief-drift`. There is no skip for a step that does not exist yet, so a default `@latest` install would mutate the operator's prefix during Phase 3 rehearsal, before the real cut. A version-pinned variant would instead poll npm for `0.0.1` indefinitely.

## And the original justification does not survive its own timeline

The argument for upgrading was that the maintainer cannot verify their own release, because `deft-hook` resolves to the global package and rebuilding locally changes nothing. **That hook-resolution fact is correct.** The conclusion that the release pipeline is the place to fix it is not.

Three mechanisms already compare installed-versus-latest and recommend `npm i -g`, and **all three skip the framework repo** by explicit condition:

- session release probe — `packages/core/src/session/release-availability.ts:121-122`, empty when `runningInsideDeftRepo`
- doctor payload-staleness — `packages/core/src/doctor/payload-staleness.ts:163-167`, `skip -- running inside deft framework repo`
- staleness tickler idle gate — `packages/core/src/staleness-tickler/idle.ts:36-37`, `reason: "framework-repo"`

The gated session ritual does not upgrade either; its execute set is `agent_hooks`, `doctor`, `cache_fresh`.

**Those skips are what permitted the twelve-version gap.** The hooks ran August code all day *before* the cut. A step that fires only after a successful release would not have prevented a single hour of it — it would merely have closed the gap after the next cut.

## Which runtime, precisely

"The release pipeline" hides three, and a default mutation means something different and wrong in each:

1. the operator's local `task release`
2. `task release:e2e`, reusing `runPipeline` at `0.0.1`
3. GitHub Actions jobs — `npm-publish.yml` (on `ubuntu-latest`, because provenance rejects self-hosted runners) and `release.yml` for installer assets

**No workflow invokes `task release` or `runPipeline`.** Whether anyone runs it on a shared runner is unverified; nothing currently does.

There is also an unweighed cost in the original shape: step 13 returns *before* `npm-publish.yml` must be green, and the release skill's Phase 5/7 already wait on that workflow and then `npm view` all four packages. A polling step inside `runPipeline` would block the operator's local command for up to fifteen minutes waiting on a job the process does not own, duplicating a wait the skill already performs.

## The two npm properties still matter — for the check

Both were observed and neither is in dispute. They are requirements on any registry read, upgrade or not.

**Propagation is not atomic across sibling packages.** `@deftai/directive` and `@deftai/directive-types` were visible at 0.107.0 while `@deftai/directive-core` was not. A direct registry read with no client cache confirmed the absence. Roughly seven minutes later all four were present. So the check must poll until **every** workspace package resolves; reading one is not sufficient evidence.

**A lag-induced failure poisons the retry.** Once the registry had all four, the upgrade still failed with an identical `ETARGET`, returning in about one second — npm never re-fetched. `--prefer-online` cleared it in ~10 s. This is the nastier half: after a lag failure, the naive retry keeps failing for a *different* reason with the *same* error text, and an operator can conclude the release is broken when it is fine.

## Acceptance

- [ ] After a release, the pipeline reports the local global CLI version, the released version, and whether they match. `runPipeline`'s completion text currently names `dry_run` / `skip_tag` / `skip_release` and says nothing about the CLI on the machine that just cut the release.
- [ ] The check polls **all four** workspace packages, bypasses the npm metadata cache, uses a bounded wait, and distinguishes "still propagating" from "publish incomplete" — those look identical today.
- [ ] Version comparison uses `checkActiveCliAgainstTarget` rather than bare `deft --version`, so a PATH-shadowed install cannot report success (#3233).
- [ ] The report includes the exact remediation command including `--prefer-online`.
- [ ] The pipeline **does not** run `npm i -g`. No global mutation, no new consent surface.
- [ ] Report-only, so no behaviour change in `release:e2e`, `--dry-run`, `--skip-tag`, `CI`, or `GITHUB_ACTIONS`. It must not block or fail the release.
- [ ] CHANGELOG `[Unreleased]` line.

## Out of scope, deliberately

- **Any default global upgrade.** Refuted above.
- **An opt-in production-cut upgrade.** May be a later increment. If ever built it must exclude `release:e2e` / `--dry-run` / `--skip-tag` / `CI` / `GITHUB_ACTIONS` / `DEFT_RELEASE_E2E`, treat the tag-push confirmation as the consent, use the active-CLI check, and fail non-fatally.
- **Lifting the framework-repo skip for global-CLI currency** — worth its own issue and arguably the more valuable half, since it is the change that would actually have caught the three-week gap on an ordinary weekday with no release involved. It changes advisory behaviour for every consumer session, not just the release path, so it should not ride along here.

## Environment

Observed on v0.107.0, 2026-08-26, Windows 11, npm 11. Release published 03:56 UTC; `directive-core` visible on the registry by roughly 04:02 UTC. All four packages now report 0.107.0 and this host's CLI reports a matching engine.

Related: #3738 (the fix that could not be verified locally), #3742 (agent-hook enforcement tracker — hooks run the global CLI, so a stale global means stale gates), #3233 (PATH shadowing after a global install).

## Non-self-arbitration disclosure

I filed this issue and I am running its triage. I may not clear my own claims. The refutation target is my own conclusion — specifically the opt-out framing in "Suggested shape" — chosen because it is the part I argued least and would most regret.

## What is well established

Both failure properties were observed rather than reasoned, and both are non-obvious:

The second is the nastier property and is the part most likely to be dropped by an implementer who only reads the first.

## Audit markers

- `audit:blast-radius` — a step that runs `npm i -g` touches state outside the repository, outside the release, and outside anything the pipeline can roll back. The body does not weigh that.
- `audit:ci-context` — the release pipeline may run somewhere other than a maintainer laptop. What a default global upgrade means on a shared runner, or in a container, is unaddressed.

## Refutation verdict

The two observed npm properties (non-atomic sibling propagation; a lag-induced `ETARGET` poisoning the retry) are out of envelope as disputed facts. I did not re-run a publish. They can stay as properties of any *check* that talks to the registry.

None of those hold at this SHA.

Treated the body's "Suggested shape" as the least-argued part, per the author's own disclosure on 5420751501.

class: `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** No workflow under `.github/workflows/` invokes `task release` or `runPipeline`. What GHA does after a `v*` tag:

- `npm-publish.yml` publishes the four packages on `ubuntu-latest` (line 31). Required there because provenance rejects self-hosted runners (comment at lines 27-30).
- `release.yml` builds Go installer assets and attaches them to the draft. Comments at 286-289 and 317 refer to `task release` as the *local* draft-create path, not as a job step.

class: `sharpens-framing`

- Staleness tickler idle gate: `reason: "framework-repo"` (`packages/core/src/staleness-tickler/idle.ts:36-37`).

An operator who skips the new step, or who cuts from a machine that is not their daily hook host, still cannot "verify their own release" via hooks.

**Disposition.** Keep the claim as "hooks execute the global package." Drop "therefore the release pipeline must upgrade it." The successor lean should choose among: (a) report local-vs-released at Phase 7 / pipeline complete, (b) lift the framework-repo skip for *global CLI currency only* (not deposit staleness), (c) an opt-in production-cut upgrade. (a) or (b) address the night; (c) is optional.

## Silence, not inaction, is the load-bearing defect

class: `sharpens-framing`

**Evidence.** Pipeline complete text reports `dry_run` / `skip_tag` / `skip_release` and nothing about the local CLI (`pipeline.ts:589`). Phase 7 already requires `npm view` on all four packages (`SKILL.md:324`) and does not compare `deft --version` / `deft-hook` resolution to the cut. That is silence on the one machine whose hooks the author could not use as a verifier.

A report that says "global CLI is 0.95.0; you just cut 0.107.0; hooks on this box are the old binary; upgrade with `npm i -g @deftai/directive@<version> --prefer-online`" needs the polling and cache-bypass machinery the body discovered. It does not need an opt-out default write.

**Road-not-taken.** I chose report-plus-optional-opt-in over default mutation. The strongest case for the default is: this operator already did not upgrade for three weeks, so a prompt will be ignored the same way, and only a write closes the loop. That steelman assumes the skip-on-framework-repo advisory layer stays blind and that e2e/CI/rollback are solved. Flip the verdict if the successor lean (1) excludes e2e/dry-run/CI, (2) treats the existing tag-push confirmation as explicit consent to also write the prefix, (3) uses `checkActiveCliAgainstTarget` not bare `--version`, and (4) makes failure non-fatal. That is no longer "opt-out default." It is a consented production-cut extra. Until those four are in the lean, the default stays blocked.

**Failure mode.** Shipping step 14 as specified trains the next implementer to put `npm i -g` inside `runPipeline` with a skip flag. The smaller change — emit the drift line where the pipeline is already silent, reuse Phase 7's all-four `npm view` — is then never considered.

**Disposition.** Bind the *check* (all four packages, cache-bypass, bounded wait, distinguish lag vs missing publish). Do not bind default mutation. Opt-in may remain as a later increment.

## Recut

**Bind the check. Do not bind the mutation.**

- Report local-versus-released where the pipeline is currently silent. `runPipeline`'s completion text names `dry_run`, `skip_tag`, and `skip_release` and says nothing about the CLI on the machine that just cut the release. That silence is the defect.
- The report needs the machinery the body did discover and that survives intact: poll **all four** packages, bypass the npm metadata cache, bound the wait, and distinguish "still propagating" from "publish incomplete." Reuse Phase 7's existing all-four `npm view`.
- Use `checkActiveCliAgainstTarget` rather than bare `deft --version`, so a PATH-shadowed install cannot report success.
- **Separately consider lifting the framework-repo skip for global-CLI currency only** — not for deposit staleness. This is the change that would actually have caught the three-week gap, on an ordinary weekday, without any release. I lean toward this being the more valuable half of the issue, and it is not in the body at all.
- An opt-in production-cut upgrade may remain as a later increment. If it is ever built it must exclude `release:e2e`, `--dry-run`, `--skip-tag`, `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, and `DEFT_RELEASE_E2E`; treat the tag-push confirmation as the consent; use the active-CLI check; and fail non-fatally.

**Reported, not verified by me:** the `runPipeline` step count and rollback surface, the `release:e2e` flag set, the three framework-repo skip sites, `GATED_STEPS`, the #3233 PATH-shadowing precedent, the sync-skill consent rule, the tickler's interactive gate, `rehearseNpmInstallAndRun`, and the absence of `task release` from any workflow. All are cited to file and line and independently checkable; I re-ran none of them.

**Verified by me, earlier in this session and consistent with the critic's footnote:** all four packages are now at 0.107.0 and this host's CLI reports a matching engine. That confirms the post-incident upgrade, not the lag the body described.

**Non-self-arbitration:** I filed this issue, ran its triage, and set its refutation target at the part I had argued least. That part broke. I am accepting the refutation whole, including the finding that my central justification would not have prevented the incident that motivated it. I cleared none of my own claims.

The recut is strictly smaller and safer than the filed proposal: a report where there was silence, no mutation, no new consent surface. The framework-repo-skip question is the one I would flag for operator attention, because it changes advisory behaviour for every consumer session rather than only the release path.
